title: The total ring of fractions of a reduced Noetherian ring is a finite product of fields
statement: Let $R$ be a reduced Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] (no nonzero nilpotent elements), let $\mathfrak q_1,\dots,\mathfrak q_t$ be its minimal prime ideals, pairwise distinct (finitely many, [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finitely-many-minimal-primes]), and let $S\subset R$ be the set of nonzerodivisors of $R$, with total ring of fractions $Q(R)=S^{-1}R$. Then: (1) for each $i$ the localization $R_{\mathfrak q_i}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a field, $\mathfrak q_iR_{\mathfrak q_i}=0$, so $R_{\mathfrak q_i}=\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)$; (2) $S\subset R\setminus\mathfrak q_i$ for each $i$, so there are unique ring maps $Q(R)\to R_{\mathfrak q_i}$ compatible with the maps from $R$, and the induced ring map $Q(R)\to R_{\mathfrak q_1}\times\cdots\times R_{\mathfrak q_t}$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 02LX (lemma-total-ring-fractions-no-embedded-points, line 4612), whose hypothesis 'q_1 u ... u q_t is the set of zerodivisors' holds for reduced R by Lemma Tag 00EW (lemma-reduced-ring-sub-product-fields, (3)); R_q a field for q minimal and R reduced: Lemma Tag 00EU (lemma-minimal-prime-reduced-ring); finiteness of minimal primes: Lemma Tag 00FR. Cited together (02LX and 00FR) in Smoothing Ring Maps, proof of Lemma Tag 07F5

proof.text: Proof of (1). Each $\mathfrak q_i$ is a minimal prime of the reduced ring $R$, so $R_{\mathfrak q_i}$ is a field and its maximal ideal $\mathfrak q_iR_{\mathfrak q_i}$ is $0$ [lem-weil-pbc-minimal-prime-reduced-localization-field]. Hence $\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)=R_{\mathfrak q_i}/\mathfrak q_iR_{\mathfrak q_i}=R_{\mathfrak q_i}/0=R_{\mathfrak q_i}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime].

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00EU (lemma-minimal-prime-reduced-ring) and its proof

proof.text: $S\subseteq R\setminus\mathfrak q_i$ and the maps $Q(R)\to R_{\mathfrak q_i}$. Since $R$ is reduced, every element of a minimal prime $\mathfrak q_i$ is a zerodivisor, and conversely every zerodivisor lies in $\mathfrak q_1\cup\dots\cup\mathfrak q_t$ [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-zerodivisors-union-minimal-primes] (the $\mathfrak q_i$ are all the minimal primes); so $R\setminus S=\mathfrak q_1\cup\dots\cup\mathfrak q_t$ and in particular $S\cap\mathfrak q_i=\emptyset$, i.e. $S\subseteq R\setminus\mathfrak q_i$. Hence every $s\in S$ maps to a unit $s/1$ of $R_{\mathfrak q_i}$, and $\phi_i:Q(R)\to R_{\mathfrak q_i}$, $r/s\mapsto (r/1)(s/1)^{-1}$, is a well-defined ring map compatible with the maps from $R$ (if $u(rs'-r's)=0$ with $u\in S$ then $u/1$ is a unit, so $(r/1)(s/1)^{-1}=(r'/1)(s'/1)^{-1}$) [def-weil-pbc-module-localization]. It is the only such ring map: a ring map $\psi$ out of $Q(R)$ is determined by $r\mapsto\psi(r/1)$, since $r/s=(r/1)(s/1)^{-1}$. Let $\phi=(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_t):Q(R)\to R_{\mathfrak q_1}\times\dots\times R_{\mathfrak q_t}$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 00EW (lemma-reduced-ring-sub-product-fields) (3), and Algebra, Lemma Tag 02LX (lemma-total-ring-fractions-no-embedded-points), proof, first two sentences

proof.text: The prime ideals of $Q(R)$. Let $\lambda:R\to Q(R)$, $r\mapsto r/1$, a localization of $R$ at $S$. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso] (1), $\mathfrak q'\mapsto\lambda^{-1}(\mathfrak q')$ is a bijection from the primes of $Q(R)$ onto the primes $\mathfrak p$ of $R$ with $\mathfrak p\cap S=\emptyset$, with inverse $\mathfrak p\mapsto\mathfrak pQ(R)$; it preserves inclusions in both directions ($\mathfrak q'=\lambda(\lambda^{-1}\mathfrak q')Q(R)$). Let $\mathfrak p$ be such a prime. Then $\mathfrak p\subseteq R\setminus S=\mathfrak q_1\cup\dots\cup\mathfrak q_t$ (Step 2), so by prime avoidance [lem-weil-pbc-prime-avoidance] (all $\mathfrak q_i$ prime) $\mathfrak p\subseteq\mathfrak q_j$ for some $j$, and $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q_j$ by minimality of $\mathfrak q_j$. Conversely each $\mathfrak q_i$ is disjoint from $S$ (Step 2). Hence the prime ideals of $Q(R)$ are exactly $\mathfrak m_i=\mathfrak q_iQ(R)$, $i=1,\dots,t$, pairwise distinct (as $\lambda^{-1}(\mathfrak m_i)=\mathfrak q_i$), with no inclusion $\mathfrak m_i\subsetneq\mathfrak m_j$ (it would give $\mathfrak q_i\subsetneq\mathfrak q_j$, against minimality of $\mathfrak q_j$). Every $\mathfrak m_i$ lies in a maximal ideal, which is prime, hence is some $\mathfrak m_j$, hence equals $\mathfrak m_i$: so $\mathfrak m_1,\dots,\mathfrak m_t$ are all maximal, and they are all the maximal ideals of $Q(R)$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 02LX (lemma-total-ring-fractions-no-embedded-points), proof, third and fourth sentences (Lemma Tag 00DS lemma-silly, Lemma Tag 00E3 lemma-spec-localization)

proof.text: $Q(R)$ is the product of its localizations at the $\mathfrak m_i$. The intersection $\mathfrak m_1\cap\dots\cap\mathfrak m_t$ is the intersection of all prime ideals of $Q(R)$ (Step 3), which is the nilradical $\sqrt{(0)}$ of $Q(R)$ [lem-weil-pbc-zero-locus-eq-iff-radical-eq] (with $I=0$); so every element of the Jacobson radical of $Q(R)$ is nilpotent. As $Q(R)$ has the finitely many maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_1,\dots,\mathfrak m_t$, the canonical map $Q(R)\to\prod_{i=1}^tQ(R)_{\mathfrak m_i}$, $x\mapsto(x/1)_i$, is an isomorphism of $Q(R)$-algebras, hence of $R$-algebras [lem-weil-pbc-product-of-localizations-at-maximal]. (For $t=0$, $R=0$, $Q(R)=0$ and both sides are the zero ring.)

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 02LX (lemma-total-ring-fractions-no-embedded-points), proof, fifth sentence: Spec Q(R) finite discrete gives Q(R) = A_1 x ... x A_t (Lemma Tag 00EM lemma-disjoint-implies-product, here in the form of Lemma Tag 00JA)

proof.text: Identification of the factors and conclusion. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-prime-residue-field-iso] (2), applied to $\lambda:R\to Q(R)$ and $\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak m_i$ (with $\lambda^{-1}(\mathfrak m_i)=\mathfrak q_i$), the map $R_{\mathfrak q_i}\to Q(R)_{\mathfrak m_i}$, $a/s\mapsto\lambda(a)/\lambda(s)$, is an isomorphism of $R$-algebras. Composing the inverses of these with the isomorphism of Step 4 gives an isomorphism of $R$-algebras $Q(R)\to R_{\mathfrak q_1}\times\dots\times R_{\mathfrak q_t}$ whose $i$-th component is a ring map $Q(R)\to R_{\mathfrak q_i}$ compatible with the maps from $R$; by the uniqueness in Step 2 it is $\phi_i$. Hence $\phi$ is this isomorphism, proving (2).
